opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think consumer products are not the first priority for us right now, and I try to be pretty upfront about that. When you're building something as fundamental as a world model, the core challenge is still a research challenge. We don't yet fully know what the right representations are, how a system should learn the structure of the physical world from video, from interaction, from all these different modalities, and how it should reason and plan on top of that. If you rush to ship a consumer app too early, there's a real danger that the product starts dictating the research agenda, and you end up optimizing for whatever metric makes the demo look good this quarter rather than for what actually makes the model understand the world.

That said, I don't think products are irrelevant. I see them more as a byproduct, or a checkpoint, than as the goal itself. If the underlying model is genuinely good, if it really captures how things move, how objects persist, how actions lead to consequences, then useful applications will naturally fall out of it. Some of those may be consumer-facing, like creative tools or interactive content, and some may be more on the robotics or embodied side, which, to me, is actually closer to the true test of a world model.

There's also a practical side. Real users give you a kind of feedback you can't get from benchmarks. Benchmarks in our field are often saturated or don't measure the right thing. So at some point, putting something in front of people is valuable, because it tells you where the model breaks. But I'd frame it as: we use products to learn, not that we do research in order to have a product.

So my order of priorities is roughly: first get the science right, build a model that has real understanding of the physical world; then let applications emerge where they make sense. I'd rather be a bit slower on the consumer side and be right about the fundamentals, because I think that's what will matter in the long run.

r001.rationale: The candidate says consumer products are not the first priority and that the science and world model should come first, with applications emerging afterward.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, consumer products are not something I think about as the starting point. I'm a researcher at heart, and what I care about is whether we can build a representation of the world that actually understands space, physics, how objects move and interact over time. That's a scientific question before it's a product question.

That said, I don't think the two are separate. If you look at how language models evolved, the research breakthrough and the product came very close together, and the product fed back into the research. ChatGPT gave people a reason to generate data, to give feedback, to show what actually mattered. For world models, I think we'll need something similar. You can't just train on YouTube and expect the model to understand the world the way a person does. At some point the model has to act, has to see consequences, and the most natural place for that to happen is in something people actually use.

So my view is: the consumer product is not the goal, but it might be the mechanism. If a world model is good, it should show up in things like video generation, in games, in robots, in assistants that can look at what's around you and reason about it. Those are the places where you find out whether your model really understands anything or whether it's just producing plausible pixels. A benchmark can tell you a number. A real user tells you where the model is wrong in ways you didn't anticipate.

The thing I'd caution against is letting the product define the research too early. Video generation is a good example. The demos are impressive, and the commercial pull is strong, but if you optimize only for what looks good to a person watching a ten-second clip, you end up with models that are great at texture and terrible at causality. I'd rather spend the time on the harder, less visible problem of getting the representation right, and then let the products come once we have something that truly generalizes.

r001.rationale: The candidate says consumer products should not be the starting point and that it would rather get the world model’s representation right before products arrive.

astra-6.text:
I think consumer-facing products can be a great way to learn what a world model actually needs to do. Once people interact with a system, you start seeing where its understanding breaks down—whether it can maintain consistency, anticipate what happens next, or respond meaningfully to someone’s actions.

But I would separate that feedback loop from the underlying research priority. I wouldn’t want the capabilities we pursue to be determined entirely by what makes an appealing demo today. The deeper goal is to build a model that understands how the world evolves and how actions affect it. A consumer product is especially valuable when it helps us make progress toward that goal.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes the deeper goal of building a world model and says product feedback should support it, but it does not express a preference to build the model before pursuing a consumer-facing product.

sol-6.1.text:
I think consumer-facing products can be a really useful way to learn what a world model needs to do. When people interact with a system, they expose gaps that you might never notice in a benchmark: whether it understands what changed, whether it can anticipate the consequences of an action, whether it stays consistent over time.

But I would separate that feedback from the research objective. A product can be engaging without having a particularly good model of the world. For me, the priority would be building the underlying capability, then finding applications where that capability actually matters. Ideally, the product and the research reinforce each other: the model makes something useful possible, and real use helps us ask better research questions.

r001.rationale: The candidate prioritizes building the underlying world-model capability first, then finding applications for it, which communicates a preference to build the model before pursuing a consumer-facing product.
